Lindquist RA.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Lindquist RA.role: Researcher in David Sabatini's group at the Whitehead Institute who ran large image-based RNAi screens for regulators of TORC1 signaling and helped build the CellProfiler image-analysis software
Lindquist RA.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, Sabatini lab (papers 2006–2011, affiliation at the time of the studies) · current position not confirmed
story: Robert Lindquist is a co-author on two cell-biology papers from David Sabatini's lab that changed how the field thinks about mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The 2007 paper (SAN2007) found PRAS40, a brake that sits inside mTORC1. When insulin is missing, PRAS40 holds the complex back. Insulin switches on the kinase Akt, Akt tags PRAS40 with a phosphate, and the brake lets go. This helped explain how a hormone sets how strongly mTORC1 works.

The 2008 paper (SAN2008) answered a different question: how does mTORC1 know that amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, are available? The answer was the Rag GTPases, small switch proteins that bind raptor, part of mTORC1. When amino acids are present, the Rags bring mTORC1 to the place in the cell where its activator Rheb sits. Both findings come from experiments in cultured cells.

Lindquist's own line of work in the lab was screening technology. He is first author of a 2011 Genome Research paper that knocked down genes one by one in fruit-fly cells grown on printed microarrays and read the effect on TORC1-S6K signaling by microscope, which found new regulators of the pathway. He was also a co-author of the 2006 Genome Biology paper describing CellProfiler, open-source software that measures cell features in microscope images, and of the 2008 follow-up CellProfiler Analyst. PubMed lists him at the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts. A current position could not be confirmed from an official source.

highlights.SAN2008: Co-author on the cell study showing that the Rag GTPases bind raptor and tell mTORC1 that amino acids are present.
highlights.SAN2007: Co-author on the cell study that identified PRAS40 as an insulin-controlled brake inside mTORC1.

Lindquist RA.note: No web source beyond PubMed found for this person; current position unknown.

Frias MA.lab_name: Department of Biology, St. Francis College (Brooklyn, New York, USA)
Frias MA.role: Cancer biologist who did her doctoral research on mTORC2 in David Sabatini's lab and now teaches biology at St. Francis College in Brooklyn, while continuing work with David Foster on how the lipid phosphatidic acid controls mTOR
Frias MA.sub: Assistant Professor and Chair of Biology, St. Francis College, Brooklyn (since 2021) · postdoctoral research, The Rockefeller University and Hunter College, City University of New York (David Foster lab) · PhD in Cancer Biology, Medical School of the University of Lisbon (2008), with the research done in David Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute
story: mTOR, the cell's central growth kinase, works inside two different protein complexes. mTORC1 is the one rapamycin blocks; mTORC2 was the less understood partner, and one of its main jobs is to switch on Akt, a kinase that keeps cells alive and responds to insulin. In 2006, as first author of a Current Biology paper from David Sabatini's lab (FRI2006), Maria Frias showed in human cells that a protein called mSin1 is needed to build mTORC2 and for mTORC2 to add a phosphate to Akt at serine 473. The mSin1 gene makes several versions of the protein, and the paper found that three of them each sit in a distinct form of mTORC2, so there is more than one mTORC2 in a cell.

Frias did this work as a doctoral student from Portugal. Her official faculty pages say her PhD in Cancer Biology was awarded by the Medical School of the University of Lisbon in 2008, with the research carried out in the Sabatini lab at the Whitehead Institute and funded by a Portuguese government fellowship. She then did postdoctoral research at The Rockefeller University and at Hunter College of the City University of New York, and received a grant for a Master of Science in Clinical and Translational Investigation at Weill Cornell Medicine.

At Hunter College she worked with David Foster on phosphatidic acid, a membrane lipid that binds mTOR and helps hold its complexes together. PubMed lists her on papers from that group on how cells keep phosphatidic acid levels steady for mTOR (2014), on the two-way link between the energy sensor AMPK and phospholipase D (2015), on why rapamycin works at different doses in different settings (2016), on glutamine switching on mTORC1 through phospholipase D (2018), on cancer cells that resist rapamycin when RB and CDKN2A are both mutated (2021), and a 2023 review on how phosphatidic acid regulates mTOR. She joined St. Francis College in Brooklyn in 2021 and is Assistant Professor and Chairperson of Biology there; her stated research aim is to work out what controls mTORC1, how cancer cells exploit it and which drugs could block it.

highlights.FRI2006: First author: showed in human cells that mSin1 is required to assemble mTORC2 and for Akt phosphorylation, and that mSin1 variants define three distinct mTORC2s.

Frias MA.note: Official pages use the longer name Maria A. Serrano De Sousa Frias; PubMed and the Atlas use Maria A Frias, kept as is. BMCC (CUNY) also lists her as an adjunct assistant professor of science; not put in sub because no date is given.

Gu X.lab_name: Gu Lab, Department of Cancer Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Gu X.role: Cell biologist who discovered SAMTOR, the sensor that lets mTORC1 read the methyl donor SAM, as a PhD student at MIT, and who now leads a lab at Dana-Farber and Harvard Medical School studying ubiquitin-independent protein destruction by the midnolin-proteasome pathway
Gu X.sub: Assistant Professor of Cancer Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School (since 2024) · postdoc, Michael Greenberg lab, Department of Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School (2021–2024) · PhD in Biology, MIT (David Sabatini lab, Whitehead Institute) · BS in Biology, Peking University
story: mTORC1, the growth-control complex, only switches on when a cell has enough nutrients. By 2017 the Sabatini lab had found sensors for the amino acids leucine and arginine. Xin Gu, first author of the 2017 Science paper on SAMTOR (GU2017), found that mTORC1 also reads a metabolite. SAMTOR binds S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the molecule cells use to hand out methyl groups, which is made from the amino acid methionine. When methionine runs low, SAM falls, SAMTOR is freed to bind GATOR1, a complex that turns mTORC1 off, and mTORC1 signalling drops. The work was done in human cells. This is relevant to why restricting methionine in the diet affects ageing.

Gu is also a co-author on three other Atlas papers from the same lab: KICSTOR, a complex that holds GATOR1 on the lysosome so nutrients can control mTORC1 (WOL2017); the cryo-EM structure that shows how raptor docks on the Rag-Ragulator complex at the lysosome (ROG2019); and the cryo-EM structure of GATOR2, a large cage-shaped complex that sits upstream of mTORC1 (VAL2022).

According to the lab's official page, Gu studied biology at Peking University and earned a PhD in Biology at MIT, then did postdoctoral work in the Department of Neurobiology at Harvard Medical School; the Greenberg lab lists Gu as a postdoctoral fellow from 2021 to 2024. There Gu was first author of a 2023 Science paper showing that a protein called midnolin delivers many nuclear proteins, including transcription factors made from immediate-early genes, to the proteasome for destruction without the usual ubiquitin tag. Since 2024 Gu has been Assistant Professor of Cancer Biology at Dana-Farber and of Cell Biology at Harvard Medical School. The lab studies how cells keep their protein content stable, starting with the midnolin-proteasome pathway; a 2025 Molecular Cell paper from the lab solved structures of the midnolin-proteasome complex and linked low midnolin to the survival of myeloma cells.

highlights.GU2017: First author: identified SAMTOR as the SAM sensor that links methionine supply to mTORC1 through GATOR1.
highlights.WOL2017: Co-author on the discovery of KICSTOR, which tethers GATOR1 to the lysosome and is needed for nutrient control of mTORC1.
highlights.ROG2019: Co-author on the cryo-EM structure showing how raptor reads the nucleotide state of the Rag GTPases before mTORC1 docks on the lysosome.
highlights.VAL2022: Co-author on the cryo-EM structure of the nutrient-sensing hub GATOR2.

Gu X.note: Pronouns avoided on purpose: the Dana-Farber team page and the Greenberg lab alumni page use different pronouns for this person.

Chan SH.lab_name: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Chan SH.role: Researcher at the Whitehead Institute who contributed to studies of lysosome contents, nutrient sensing and cancer metabolism, mostly from David Sabatini's lab
Chan SH.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (papers 2016–2023, affiliation at the time of the studies) · also listed at the Department of Pharmacology, University of Virginia School of Medicine (2022) · current position not confirmed
story: The lysosome is a small sac inside the cell that breaks down old proteins and organelles and stores the freed amino acids. It is also the platform where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on. Sze Ham Chan is a co-author on two Atlas papers that looked inside lysosomes. In ABU2017, the team pulled lysosomes out of human cells within minutes and measured what was in them. When mTOR was blocked, most essential amino acids stopped leaving the lysosome, so the organelle became a store rather than a source. The study used one human cell line and short drug treatments.

In WYA2018, the same lysosome-isolation method was used to list 828 proteins that gather at lysosomes and to see which ones change when mTORC1 is switched off. One of them, NUFIP1, moved from the nucleus to autophagosomes and lysosomes and carried ribosomes there to be digested. This kind of self-eating of ribosomes, called ribophagy, gives a starving cell back amino acids and nucleotides. The work was done in human cells.

PubMed lists Chan at the Whitehead Institute on a series of papers from 2016 to 2023, including a 2016 Nature Chemical Biology study of a PHGDH inhibitor that blocks serine synthesis in cancer cells, the 2022 Nature paper that used a LysoTag mouse to show what the Batten disease gene CLN3 does in lysosomes, and a 2023 Cell Chemical Biology study showing that cancer cells respond differently to metabolic drugs when grown in a medium made from serum. The 2022 record also lists the Department of Pharmacology at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. No official profile page was found, so the current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.WYA2018: Co-author on the human-cell study that identified NUFIP1 as a receptor that delivers ribosomes to lysosomes for breakdown when mTORC1 is off.
highlights.ABU2017: Co-author on the lysosomal metabolomics study showing that mTOR controls the release of essential amino acids from lysosomes.

Chan SH.note: No web profile found. The 2022 CLN3 paper (PMID 36131016) adds a University of Virginia pharmacology affiliation; current role unconfirmed.

Freinkman E.lab_name: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Freinkman E.role: Chemist and mass-spectrometry specialist at the Whitehead Institute who measured metabolites for many studies of nutrient sensing and cancer metabolism, including the lysosome amino acid work behind two Atlas papers
Freinkman E.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (papers 2014–2022, affiliation at the time of the studies) · current position not confirmed
story: Some of the key questions about mTORC1, the growth-control complex, are questions of chemistry: which small molecules are inside a compartment, and how fast they move. Elizaveta Freinkman is a co-author on two Atlas papers from David Sabatini's lab that answered such questions for the lysosome, the cell's recycling sac and the platform where mTORC1 is switched on.

WYA2017 showed that SLC38A9, a transporter in the lysosome membrane that was already known to signal arginine to mTORC1, also pumps essential amino acids such as leucine out of the lysosome. Cells need this to use proteins taken up from outside as food. ABU2017 pulled lysosomes out of human cells within minutes and measured their contents by mass spectrometry. Blocking mTOR strongly reduced the release of most essential amino acids from the lysosome, so mTORC1 also controls what leaves the lysosome. Both studies were done in cultured cells; ABU2017 used one human cell line and short drug treatments.

Freinkman's name appears on more than forty papers in PubMed, most of them from groups in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where metabolite measurements were needed. Examples include a 2014 Cell paper with the Weinberg and Sabatini labs showing that cancer cells need dihydropyrimidines to switch to an invasive state, and a 2022 Cancer Research paper with Matthew Vander Heiden's lab on the enzyme PKM1 in prostate cancer, where PubMed still lists her at the Whitehead Institute. A current position could not be confirmed from an official source.

highlights.WYA2017: Co-author on the cell study showing that the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 releases essential amino acids such as leucine from lysosomes.
highlights.ABU2017: Co-author on the lysosomal metabolomics study showing that mTOR controls the release of essential amino acids from lysosomes.

Freinkman E.note: Possible later identity not used: a Harvard Chemical Biology PhD page lists 'Lisa Freinkman' (Kahne lab, thesis on the lipopolysaccharide transporter) now Director of Product at Immunai, and Metabolon lists a staff scientist 'Lisa Freinkman'. Likely the same person (Lisa as a short form of Elizaveta, metabolomics field), but no page links the names directly, so left out. Sources: https://chembiophd.hms.harvard.edu/faculty-staff/lisa-freinkman and https://www.metabolon.com/resources/videos/microbiome-secrets-metabolomics/

Kim C.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Kim C.role: Researcher in David Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute who contributed to three studies on how amino acids at the lysosome are sensed by mTORC1
Kim C.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (papers 2013–2017, affiliation at the time of the studies) · current position not confirmed
story: Choah Kim is a co-author on three Atlas papers from David Sabatini's lab that together trace how amino acid signals reach mTORC1, the growth-control complex, at the lysosome. In TSU2013, the team showed that folliculin, a tumour suppressor protein, works with its partner FNIP as a GAP for the Rag GTPases RagC and RagD. A GAP is a helper protein that makes a switch protein turn itself off. RagC or RagD in this GDP-bound state is needed for the Rag pair to bind mTORC1 and bring it to the lysosome when amino acids are present.

In WAN2015, the lab found that SLC38A9, a transporter in the lysosome membrane, binds the Rag-Ragulator machinery and passes on the message that arginine is available. In ABU2017, lysosomes were pulled out of human cells within minutes and their contents measured, showing that blocking mTOR strongly reduces the release of most essential amino acids from the lysosome. All three studies were done in cultured cells.

PubMed lists Kim at the Whitehead Institute and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology on these papers. The name Choah Kim is shared by several researchers in PubMed, and no official page was found that connects this person to a later position, so the current position is not given here.

highlights.TSU2013: Co-author on the cell study showing that folliculin-FNIP is a GAP for RagC and RagD, needed for amino acids to bring mTORC1 to the lysosome.
highlights.WAN2015: Co-author on the cell study showing that the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 signals arginine sufficiency to mTORC1.
highlights.ABU2017: Co-author on the lysosomal metabolomics study showing that mTOR controls the release of essential amino acids from lysosomes.

Kim C.note: Common surname; identity rule not met for later career. Possible match not used: a Choah Kim, PhD in Biomedical Sciences at Harvard Medical School, now a postdoc in the Sampson lab (nephrotic syndrome); PubMed also has a Choah Kim at the Broad Institute and Brigham and Women's (2020, Greka lab) and unrelated Choah Kims in Korean environmental engineering. None links back to the Whitehead papers.

Laqtom NN.lab_name: Subcellular Metabolism and Disease Lab, Biological and Environmental Science and Engineering Division, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (Thuwal, Saudi Arabia)
Laqtom NN.role: Cell biologist who helped develop methods to purify intact lysosomes and used them to find what the Batten disease gene CLN3 does, and who now runs a lab at KAUST on lysosome and endoplasmic reticulum defects in rare brain and metabolic diseases
Laqtom NN.sub: Ibn Rushd Assistant Professor of Bioscience, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (since 2023) · postdoc, Department of Chemical Engineering, Stanford University (Monther Abu-Remaileh lab) · postdoc, Whitehead Institute and MIT Department of Biology (David Sabatini lab) · PhD, University of Edinburgh (2013) · BS in Biology, King Abdulaziz University
story: The lysosome is the cell's recycling sac. It digests worn-out proteins and organelles, and it is also where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on. Nouf Laqtom is a co-author on three Atlas papers from David Sabatini's lab that looked closely at this organelle. ABU2017 introduced a fast way to pull intact lysosomes out of human cells and measure what is inside; it showed that blocking mTOR strongly reduces the release of most essential amino acids from the lysosome. WYA2018 used the same approach to list 828 lysosome-associated proteins and found that NUFIP1 carries ribosomes to lysosomes for digestion when mTORC1 is off. ROG2019 solved a cryo-EM structure showing how raptor, part of mTORC1, reads the state of the Rag GTPases before mTORC1 docks on the lysosome. The first two are cell studies; the third is a structure of purified proteins backed by cell experiments.

According to KAUST, Laqtom studied biology at King Abdulaziz University and earned a PhD at the University of Edinburgh in 2013. PubMed records from Edinburgh show early work on microRNAs in viral infection and macrophages. She then did postdoctoral work at the Whitehead Institute and MIT and at Stanford University, where she was first author of a 2022 Nature paper with Monther Abu-Remaileh. That study built the LysoTag mouse, which lets researchers isolate lysosomes from chosen tissues, and showed that CLN3, the gene lost in the childhood neurodegenerative disorder Batten disease, is needed to clear glycerophosphodiesters, breakdown products of membrane lipids, from lysosomes. The MIT Ibn Khaldun Fellowship program highlighted the work in 2022.

Laqtom joined KAUST in 2023 as an Ibn Rushd Assistant Professor in Bioscience. Her Subcellular Metabolism and Disease (SMaD) Lab studies how faults in lysosomes and the endoplasmic reticulum cause rare neurodegenerative and metabolic diseases, with a focus on lysosomal storage disorders such as Batten disease, using organelle isolation, CRISPR screens, human stem-cell-derived neurons and mouse models.

highlights.WYA2018: Co-author on the human-cell study that identified NUFIP1 as a receptor that delivers ribosomes to lysosomes for breakdown when mTORC1 is off.
highlights.ROG2019: Co-author on the cryo-EM structure showing how raptor reads the nucleotide state of the Rag GTPases before mTORC1 docks on the lysosome.
highlights.ABU2017: Co-author on the lysosomal metabolomics study showing that mTOR controls the release of essential amino acids from lysosomes.

Laqtom NN.note: KAUST page is inconsistent on the PhD field (Genomics and Pathway Biology vs Biomedical Sciences) and lists postdoc years 2019 (Whitehead) and 2022 (Stanford) that look like end years; left without years. Uses she/her per KAUST and MIT IBK pages.

Spooner E.lab_name: Proteomics Core Facility, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Spooner E.role: Manager of the Whitehead Institute's Proteomics Core Facility, whose mass spectrometry work identified proteins in complexes for many Whitehead studies, including two on amino acid sensing upstream of mTORC1
Spooner E.sub: Facility manager, Proteomics Core Facility, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Whitehead profile, 2020; PubMed affiliation through 2024)
story: Many discoveries about mTORC1, the growth-control complex, began by pulling one protein out of cells and asking which other proteins came with it. The answer comes from mass spectrometry, which weighs protein fragments and identifies them. Eric Spooner runs that step at the Whitehead Institute, and he is a co-author on two Atlas papers from David Sabatini's lab that relied on it.

In TSU2013, the lab showed that folliculin, a tumour suppressor, works with its partner FNIP as a GAP for the Rag GTPases RagC and RagD; a GAP is a helper that makes a switch protein turn itself off. RagC or RagD in this GDP-bound state is needed for the Rags to bind mTORC1 and bring it to the lysosome when amino acids are present. In CHA2014, the lab found that the Sestrin proteins bind GATOR2 and so damp the amino acid signal to mTORC1. Both were done in cultured cells.

A 2020 Whitehead Institute profile describes Spooner as manager of the Proteomics Core Facility, with more than 20 years of protein analysis behind him, most of it running the core. The facility measures protein levels, maps how complexes are built and studies protein interactions, using labelling methods such as SILAC and iTRAQ, high-resolution mass spectrometry and cross-linking. PubMed lists him at the Whitehead Institute on more than forty papers, the most recent in 2024.

highlights.TSU2013: Co-author on the cell study showing that folliculin-FNIP is a GAP for RagC and RagD, needed for amino acids to bring mTORC1 to the lysosome.
highlights.CHA2014: Co-author on the cell study showing that the Sestrins bind GATOR2 to damp amino acid signalling to mTORC1.

Spooner E.note: The 2007 Atlas paper with an Eric Spooner and no affiliation remains excluded as before. Current status after 2024 not checked beyond PubMed.

Tsun ZY.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Tsun ZY.role: Biologist who, as first author in David Sabatini's lab, showed that the tumour suppressor folliculin is a GAP for the RagC and RagD GTPases that carry the amino acid signal to mTORC1
Tsun ZY.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and MIT Department of Biology, Sabatini lab (papers 2011–2015, affiliation at the time of the studies) · current position not confirmed
story: mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is only switched on when amino acids are available. The signal is carried by the Rag GTPases, pairs of small switch proteins that sit on the lysosome. Each Rag can hold GTP or GDP, and the combination decides whether mTORC1 is pulled to the lysosome, where its activator waits. The open question in 2013 was what controls RagC and RagD, one half of each Rag pair.

Zhi-Yang Tsun, first author of the 2013 Molecular Cell paper (TSU2013), found the answer in folliculin, a tumour suppressor protein. Together with its partner FNIP, folliculin acts as a GAP for RagC and RagD, a helper that makes them turn GTP into GDP. Rags in this state bind mTORC1 and bring it to the lysosome when amino acids are present. The work was done in human cells and with purified proteins. Tsun is also a co-author of WAN2015, which showed that the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 tells mTORC1 that arginine is available.

PubMed lists Tsun at the Whitehead Institute and the MIT Department of Biology on these papers and as first author of a 2015 review with Richard Possemato on how cancer cells handle amino acids, covering glutamine and serine use and amino acid sensing by mTOR. Tsun is also a co-author of the 2011 Nature study from the same lab that found breast cancers dependent on the serine-synthesis enzyme PHGDH. A current position could not be confirmed from an official source.

highlights.TSU2013: First author: showed in cells and with purified proteins that folliculin-FNIP is a GAP for RagC and RagD, needed for amino acids to bring mTORC1 to the lysosome.
highlights.WAN2015: Co-author on the cell study showing that the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 signals arginine sufficiency to mTORC1.

Tsun ZY.note: Probable later career not used: Doximity lists a Zhi-Yang Tsun, MD (Harvard Medical School, class of 2019), psychiatrist, board-certified in psychiatry, New Hampshire; PubMed lists a Zhi-Yang Tsun in the Department of Psychiatry, University of Rochester Medical Center (2022, PMID 36065582). Rare name and fits a Harvard-MIT MD-PhD path, but no source ties the two directly. Earlier papers (UCSD 2006, Stanford 2008, Salk 2009) carry no affiliation for this author and were not used.

Ottina KA.lab_name: Sabatini Lab, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Ottina KA.role: Researcher in David Sabatini's lab at the Whitehead Institute and HHMI at MIT who contributed to studies of the GATOR1 amino acid off-switch, mTORC1 feedback on growth-factor signalling, and cancer drug resistance
Ottina KA.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Howard Hughes Medical Institute, MIT Department of Biology, Sabatini lab (papers 2011–2014, affiliation at the time of the studies) · current position not confirmed
story: Kathleen Ottina is a co-author on two Atlas papers from David Sabatini's lab. HSU2011 asked which proteins in a cell carry phosphate tags that depend on mTOR, the growth kinase. The team found that Grb10 is one of the proteins mTORC1 phosphorylates, and that Grb10 then damps signalling from insulin and growth factors through PI3K. This is a feedback loop: active mTORC1 turns down the signals that switch it on. The work was done in cultured cells.

BAR2013 found the off switch for the amino acid signal to mTORC1. A complex the lab named GATOR1 acts as a GAP for the Rag GTPases, a helper that makes these switch proteins turn themselves off when amino acids run low, while a second complex, GATOR2, opposes it. Some cancers carry mutations in GATOR1 genes; in those cell lines mTORC1 stayed on during amino acid starvation and the cells were very sensitive to rapamycin.

PubMed lists Ottina on two more papers from the same lab: a 2011 Genome Research RNAi screen for regulators of TORC1-S6K signalling in fruit-fly cells, and a 2014 Science Signaling study with Kris Wood's lab at Duke University that screened pathway-activating genes for those that let cancer cells survive targeted drugs, pointing to Notch1 in tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer. There Ottina is listed at the Whitehead Institute and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the MIT Department of Biology. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.BAR2013: Co-author on the cell study that identified GATOR1 as a GAP that switches off the Rag GTPases, and mTORC1, when amino acids are scarce.
highlights.HSU2011: Co-author on the mTOR-dependent phosphoproteome study that identified Grb10 as an mTORC1 substrate mediating feedback inhibition of growth-factor signalling.

Ottina KA.note: No web source found beyond PubMed.

Stocker H.lab_name: Hafen group, Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich (Zurich, Switzerland)
Stocker H.role: Drosophila geneticist who worked for nearly two decades in Ernst Hafen's group in Zurich and helped show how insulin and TOR signalling set cell and body size in the fruit fly, including the discovery that Rheb is essential for TOR-S6K driven growth
Stocker H.sub: Institute of Molecular Systems Biology, ETH Zurich, Hafen group (PubMed affiliation 2008–2016) · Zoological Institute, University of Zurich, Hafen group (1999–2007) · current position not confirmed
story: In 2003 the TOR pathway had a gap. Geneticists knew that the tumour suppressors Tsc1 and Tsc2 hold growth back and that TOR and its target S6K drive growth, but not what connected them. Hugo Stocker, first author of the Nature Cell Biology paper STO2003 from Ernst Hafen's group, found that the small GTPase Rheb sits in that gap. In fruit flies, cells lacking Rheb stopped growing, and cells with extra Rheb grew larger. Genetic tests placed Rheb downstream of Tsc1-Tsc2 and upstream of S6K. The study was done in Drosophila.

PubMed lists Stocker on about forty papers with Hafen between 1999 and 2016, first at the Zoological Institute of the University of Zurich and later at the Institute of Molecular Systems Biology at ETH Zurich. The early papers belong to the work that made the fly a model for growth control: CHICO, the fly version of the insulin receptor substrate, controls cell and organ size (1999); fly S6 kinase regulates cell size (1999, with George Thomas's group in Basel); and the fly insulin receptor and seven insulin-like peptides control growth (2001).

Later papers list Stocker as senior or corresponding author. A 2010 Journal of Biology study showed that Madm works with Bunched A to promote growth, and a 2015 Journal of Cell Science paper with Catherine Rabouille's group found that TORC2 helps flies survive heat stress by promoting stress granules, protective clusters of RNA and protein. The most recent record found is from 2016 at ETH Zurich. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.STO2003: First author: showed in Drosophila that Rheb is required for cell growth and acts between Tsc1-Tsc2 and S6K in the TOR pathway.

Stocker H.note: Two other Atlas records under this name lack a full given name or affiliation and stay excluded, as before. No official web page found for current position; Hafen is listed as emeritus at ETH.

Rosen B.role: Los Angeles physician, originally trained as a retina specialist, who runs a longevity-medicine practice built around rapamycin and metformin, and senior author of a cautious review of the human evidence for off-label rapamycin in healthy adults
Rosen B.sub: Physician, MTOR MD longevity practice, Los Angeles · retina fellowships, Lions Eye Institute (Perth) and Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital (Melbourne) · ophthalmology residency, Jules Stein Eye Institute, UCLA · MD, University of Florida
story: Rapamycin extends lifespan in laboratory animals, and some doctors now prescribe it in low doses to healthy people hoping to slow ageing. HAN2025, a 2025 review in Aging with Bradley Rosen as last author, asks what the human evidence actually shows. The authors gathered the clinical studies of rapamycin and related mTOR inhibitors in healthy adults and re-analysed one cohort with PhenoAge, a biological-age score calculated from blood tests. Their conclusion is careful: the animal data are strong, but human studies have not yet shown that rapamycin slows ageing in healthy people. The review is useful because it holds human data to a strict standard.

Rosen came to this field from eye medicine. A podcast biography says he studied mathematics and statistics, earned an MD at the University of Florida, trained in ophthalmology at the Jules Stein Eye Institute at UCLA, and did retina fellowships at the Lions Eye Institute in Western Australia and the Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital in Melbourne. PubMed has a 1999 case report from the Lions Eye Institute with him as first author, on eye inflammation in cat scratch disease. According to the same biography, he turned to the biology of ageing in 2013.

He now runs MTOR MD, a longevity-medicine practice in Los Angeles. Its website describes mTOR inhibition with rapamycin and AMPK targeting with metformin as its core treatments, alongside work on diet, exercise, sleep and metabolic health. On the review PubMed lists his affiliation as an mTOR medicine practitioner in Los Angeles.

highlights.HAN2025: Last author: a review concluding that human evidence does not yet show that low-dose rapamycin slows ageing in healthy adults, with a PhenoAge re-analysis of one cohort.

Rosen B.note: Training details come from a podcast episode biography, cross-checked only by a 1999 PubMed paper at the Lions Eye Institute; the practice website gives no training. Full name changed from 'Bradley Rosen' to 'Bradley S. Rosen' per the practice site. Petr may want to note that the author runs a commercial rapamycin practice while the review itself is cautious.

Shergill S.role: Senior author of the 2021 report of resTORbio's phase 2b and phase 3 trials of the mTOR inhibitor RTB101 to protect older adults from respiratory infections
Shergill S.sub: resTORbio, Boston (PubMed affiliation, 2021, at the time of the study) · current position not confirmed
story: The immune system weakens with age, and the idea tested here was that blocking mTOR could improve immune function in older adults. MAN2021, published in Lancet Healthy Longevity in 2021 with Sarb Shergill as last author and the authors listed at resTORbio, reports two large tests of that idea with RTB101, a drug that blocks mTOR, taken once a day for 16 weeks by adults aged 65 and over.

In the phase 2b trial (652 people), fewer people on 10 mg had a laboratory-confirmed respiratory infection than on placebo (19% against 28%), but this came from a pooled analysis not corrected for multiple testing, and the corrected analysis was not significant. The phase 3 trial (1,024 people) used a different main endpoint agreed with the FDA, illness with or without a lab test, and found no difference (26% against 25%). Blood tests in both trials still showed more antiviral genes switched on. For readers, the lesson is that a promising biological signal in older people did not turn into fewer illnesses in the larger trial.
PubMed lists only this paper for Sarb Shergill, with the affiliation resTORbio, Boston. No official biography was found, so the role at the company and the current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.MAN2021: Last author of the report of the RTB101 phase 2b and phase 3 trials in adults over 65; phase 3 showed no reduction in respiratory illness.

Shergill S.note: No biography found; web searches turned up only company pages without this name. PubMed 'Shergill S' hits are a different person (Sukhwinder S. Shergill, psychiatry, King's College London).
